A world worth returning to

Curate a systematic body of work

Produce a systematic body of work that shows understanding of art making conventions and ideas within painting

  • AS91321 · v2
  • 12 credits
  • External
  • Painting focus

Suggested teaching time
14–18 weeks

Timing, task steps and quantities are classroom suggestions, not NZQA grade requirements.

Read the standard (PDF)

The brief

What can I discover by returning to one personally meaningful world?

Choose a personal subject-world: a familiar route, a domestic space, a collection of objects or another context you can investigate directly. Build a systematic painting inquiry in which related works generate and develop ideas. Curate the body so viewers can follow the decisions and discoveries.

Materials & preparation

Your own source imagery and drawings, a visual diary, appropriate painting media and supports, and two portfolio panels for the physical painting route.

Use your own drawings and photographs as starting points. Record sources and seek permission for people, places and culturally significant material. Discuss tikanga and context with your teacher where relevant.

This is an external standard. Use the activities as teaching suggestions; make your own decisions during assessed work. Your teacher must keep support within NZQA’s annual conditions.

Suggested size & quantity

Use these ranges to plan your studio time and materials with your teacher. They are classroom suggestions, not NZQA minimums, maximums or grade requirements. Adapt them to your idea, working pace and access needs.

Selected portfolio works

As a planning guide, aim for about 12–18 selected drawings and paintings across the whole body. One possible mix is 6–10 A6–A5 investigations, 4–6 A4 developments and 2 A3 later works. These are totals across the portfolio, not targets for each panel.

Working diary

Allow about 12–18 A3 pages, or 24–36 A4 pages, over the inquiry for sources, trials, artist connections, evaluations and records of work made separately. Some studies may become selected portfolio works; the diary is not another set of finished paintings.

Scale & selection

Lay out paper placeholders on full-size mock-ups of the two panels specified below before making larger works. Adjust the mix for margins and spacing, retaining the works that show progression. Keep the diary available for process records; do not assume it is an additional submitted panel.

One workbook page means one side of a sheet; a two-page spread counts as two pages. A3 is 297 × 420 mm, A4 is 210 × 297 mm, A5 is 148 × 210 mm and A6 is 105 × 148 mm. Two A4 pages offer about the same area as one A3 page for planning; this does not change any external submission format. Mount small studies or use clear photographs of separate works rather than making everything twice.

Artist connections

Choose the connections that serve your intention. The contemporary models offer different approaches; select a relevant comparison rather than studying every artist. These works are references, not assessment exemplars.

Compare three ways of returning to a subject: memory and place, a repeated garden inquiry, and layered spatial investigation. Choose a sustained line of inquiry that can change through making.

  • Star Gossage

    Contemporary Māori · Aotearoa New Zealand

    Gossage’s figures, colour and material choices connect with whānau, whakapapa and her ancestral home at Pākiri. Investigate how a painting can communicate remembered presence rather than a purely literal likeness.

    The Arts Foundation Te Tumu Toi · artist profile · Painting investigation

  • Karl Maughan

    Contemporary · Aotearoa New Zealand

    Maughan returns to gardens through saturated colour and carefully organised planting forms. Compare how repeated attention to one subject can produce different spatial relationships rather than a single repeated solution.

    Gow Langsford · artist profile and garden paintings · Painting investigation

  • Julie Mehretu

    Contemporary · Ethiopia / United States

    Mehretu’s layered abstractions bring drawing and painting into dialogue with place, history and movement. Follow how overlapping marks and structures can make several spatial readings coexist.

    Whitney Museum · survey, paintings and resources · Painting investigation

  • Frances Hodgkins

    Aotearoa New Zealand / Britain

    Look at how still-life objects and landscape can share a painted space. Try shifting the relationship between an object, its surroundings and its colour.

    Christchurch Art Gallery · Still Life

Historical comparison

Artwork reproduction rights and assessment permission are different. A reusable image on this site is not automatically suitable for your assessed portfolio. Read the external conditions.

Studio sequence

Use this as a flexible route through the learning. Let the work suggest the next move.

  1. Open a focused inquiry

    Identify a question worth returning to and gather your own visual sources. Investigate relevant established practices. Start with drawings and paint trials that open several plausible directions.

  2. Generate related starting points

    Explore different compositions, spatial relationships and methods. Identify the most useful possibilities for your question. Keep a record of why a particular direction deserves further work.

  3. Develop and extend

    Build related groups of paintings. Analyse what each group contributes, then use its findings in the next. Try a meaningful change that extends the idea rather than producing unrelated experiments.

  4. Clarify and revisit

    Review the developing body. Return to an earlier useful idea and reform it in response to what you now know. Where appropriate, use that return to generate a fresh line of work.

  5. Select and sequence

    Edit the works into an intelligible body. Test whether each work contributes to the progression. Complete and present the work in the current NZQA format, documenting the actual paint surfaces clearly.

A useful studio conversation

Put two related works side by side. Describe what changed, show the evidence and explain what you will investigate next. Invite feedback, then make your own decision.

Use this to review your work. Completing the list does not guarantee a grade.

0 of 3 evidence checks complete

Presentation & submission

For the 2026 painting route, present two hinged portrait panels, each 820 × 610 mm. The teacher grades the work and selected portfolios are photographed for NZQA verification. This is digital submission of the physical portfolio, not physical dispatch. An actual time-based moving-image option is limited to 120 seconds.

Read the full 2026 NZQA specifications (PDF) and external assessment conditions. These are year-specific requirements; confirm any updates for your assessment year.

What changes between grades?

Student-friendly guidance adapted from the standard. The whole body of relevant evidence determines the grade; the examples below illustrate possibilities.

Grade distinctions for AS91321
GradeWhat the evidence needs to show
AchievementOrganise related works so generation and development are visible.In this task: Editing and sequencing help the viewer follow the inquiry.
MeritBuild a purposeful body that also extends ideas.In this task: Selected works take useful discoveries further for a clear artistic purpose.
ExcellenceCreate a fluent body through critical selection, clarification and regeneration.In this task: Returning to earlier discoveries leads to convincing new work within a coherent inquiry.

Authority: NZQA AS91321 achievement criteria and explanatory notes (PDF).

Watch for

Filling two panels is a presentation task; the assessment evidence is the progression of ideas and conventions.

Pause & reflect

Which work makes the next step possible? Remove any work that adds volume without helping the inquiry progress.

Planning, assessment & differentiation

This is an external standard with school grading and NZQA verification in 2026. Use the current specification and submission instructions, not an older physical-dispatch routine. The sequence is an optional teaching approach; students must make their own developmental decisions and portfolio selections within permitted assistance.

Support and stretch

For teaching practice, reduce the number of simultaneous choices, model one material process and invite oral discussion alongside drawing. Offer vocabulary prompts and accessible media. To extend the learning, ask students to compare alternatives, justify a rejection or investigate a consequence of their own decision. Adapt assessed support to the standard’s conditions and any approved arrangements.

Before issuing the task

Set local start and finish dates, agree available materials and check the current standard, conditions and exemplars. Use school authenticity processes and your normal moderation procedures. Adjust this brief to the class and context; it has not been quality assured by NZQA.
